text: And that's the sign of a well-designed product. Nobody notices it until it's the wrong height, or it's fogged up, or a server can't reach over it, or a health inspector writes it up. Then suddenly it matters a great deal.

speaker: NORA
text: Today's company builds that piece of glass, and the counters around it. Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time and look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: NORA
text: Okay, I want to understand the product properly. What is a food shield for?
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: The basic job is to stop customers' breath, sneezes, coughs, hair and hands from contaminating food on display, while still letting them see the food and reach it. That's why the trade calls them sneeze guards. There's a popular story that the sneeze guard was invented in the late nineteen-fifties by a restaurant owner who was bothered by customers sniffing food at his buffet. Whether every detail of that story is true, I can't vouch for, but it's widely told.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: It sounds simple. A piece of glass on two posts.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: It sounds simple, and the cheap ones are. But a good food shield has to solve several problems at once. It has to be at the right height and depth for the person on the other side, whether that's an adult standing, a child, or someone in a wheelchair. It has to protect the food from above and from the front. It has to let staff reach in to refill pans. It has to be easy to clean. And it has to meet the food-safety standards the local health inspector will check.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: Tell me about those standards.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: In the United States, food equipment is commonly certified to standards from NSF, an independent organisation that writes and certifies against food equipment standards. NSF has published guidance on food shield certification requirements, covering things like the dimensions and positioning of a shield relative to the food and the customer. Local health codes, which are often based on the federal model food code, then expect equipment to be certified. I'm describing this in general terms, not giving advice on any specific rule.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: So certification is a barrier to entry.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and that's a point in favour of established suppliers like Brass Smith. A new entrant can't just cut a sheet of acrylic and sell it to hospitals. It has to design to the standard, get certified and convince buyers it's compliant.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: And there are different types?
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: Quite a few, based on the catalogues we looked at. There are shields for self-service buffets and food bars, where customers serve themselves. There are full-service shields for cafeteria lines and carving stations, where staff serve from behind and the shield protects the food from the customer side. There are freestanding countertop shields that sit on a table, and breath shields integrated into custom counters. The materials range from acrylic to tempered glass, with stainless steel or brass-finish posts and brackets.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: Brass-finish. Is that where the name comes from?
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find the origin of the name, so I won't claim that. But it would be a reasonable guess that metal fabrication is part of the heritage.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: Acrylic or glass. Does it matter which?
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: It does, and the trade-offs are general knowledge. Acrylic is lighter, cheaper and less likely to shatter, which is helpful for portable shields. But it scratches more easily and can cloud with harsh cleaning. Tempered glass is heavier and costs more, but it stays clear, resists scratches and looks more premium, which is why you see it on high-end counters. Curved tempered glass, like the Atlas Metal listing we saw, is about looks as much as function.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: So the material choice is part of the design conversation.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: Very much. A university that wants a modern food hall look may choose glass and metal finishes. A school cafeteria on a tight budget may choose acrylic. A good supplier helps the customer pick the right one for how the space will be used and cleaned. And every one of those choices changes the price.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: And I assume demand jumped in 2020.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, yes. During the pandemic, demand for clear barriers of all kinds shot up, from shop counters to offices. Self-service buffets were also shut or reformatted for a time. We didn't find anything about how that affected Brass Smith specifically, so I'd only say the whole category went through a big swing in both directions.
chapter: What a food shield actually does

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned patents. What do they cover?
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: JAMES
text: We found three United States patents in what looks like one family. The titles are "Adjustable food shield", "Adjustable food shield with detents", and "Food shield with adjustable panel". So the theme is clear. Brass Smith has protected designs that let a food shield's panels be adjusted, with detents.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: NORA
text: Detents?
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: JAMES
text: A detent is a mechanism that holds something in a set position until you push it past a click. Think of the notches on a car seat recliner, or the clicks on a camera dial. In a food shield, detents would let staff move a panel between defined positions and have it stay there securely.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: NORA
text: Why would you want to adjust a food shield?
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: JAMES
text: Think about a university dining hall. At breakfast a station is self-service, and the shield needs to protect food from customers reaching in. At lunch the same station is staffed, and the server needs to reach over or under it. Or a hotel converts a buffet into a served station for a private event. An adjustable shield lets one piece of equipment work in more than one mode, while staying within the certified positions.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: NORA
text: So flexibility for the operator.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: JAMES
text: Flexibility, and potentially fewer pieces of equipment to buy. That's a genuine customer benefit. Competitors have clearly seen the same need, because Advance Tabco, for example, has announced what it calls a convertible food shield. So adjustability is a battleground, and Brass Smith's patents give it some protected ground.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: NORA
text: How strong is that protection?
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: JAMES
text: I can't judge patent strength from titles, and nobody should take this as legal analysis. In general, patents expire about twenty years after filing, and competitors can sometimes design around them. We found no litigation. So I'd call the patents a real asset, but not a permanent moat.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: NORA
text: And the counters?
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: JAMES
text: Custom counters are a different kind of business. Standard shields can be sold off a catalogue in set sizes. A custom counter is designed for a specific space. The customer has a dining room of a particular shape, a menu, a flow of people, utility connections for hot and cold wells, and an aesthetic. The supplier has to design it, quote it, build it and deliver it. That's a project, not a product.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: NORA
text: And projects are slower.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: JAMES
text: Slower, more labour-intensive, and usually higher value per order. They also need engineering and estimating skills, which brings us to where we think the biggest AI opportunity is. But let's do the market first.
chapter: Inside the product: adjustability and patents

speaker: NORA
text: Who's the buyer in a typical deal?

speaker: JAMES
text: It depends on the product. For a standard shield, it might be a kitchen manager ordering online from a distributor like WebstaurantStore, or a dealer adding it to an equipment order. The decision is about size, finish, certification, price and delivery time.

speaker: NORA
text: And for a custom counter?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, a lot more people are involved. A foodservice consultant or designer may draw the layout. An equipment dealer may handle the order and installation. The operator, say a hospital's food and nutrition director, or a contract caterer's regional manager, has the final say on budget and style. An architect or general contractor may be in the loop if it's part of a renovation.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a long chain.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's long, and each link wants something different. The designer wants accurate drawings and specifications they can drop into their plans. The dealer wants fast, reliable quotes and a margin. The operator wants something that looks good, works on day one and passes inspection. The contractor wants it to arrive when promised and fit the space.

speaker: NORA
text: Where does a supplier win or lose?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, speed and accuracy of the quote is a big one. If a dealer asks three suppliers for a price on a custom serving line, the one that comes back first with a clear drawing and a confident number has an advantage. The one that takes three weeks may lose the job before it's even considered.

speaker: NORA
text: And the distributor channel for standard products?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's more about catalogue quality and price. Online distributors list thousands of items. Buyers filter by size and price. Clear specifications, good images and competitive pricing matter. And because buyers can compare dozens of shields side by side, standard sizes face constant price pressure.

speaker: NORA
text: Is this business seasonal?

speaker: JAMES
text: We didn't find anything specific, but in general, institutional projects often cluster around budget cycles and quiet periods. Universities, for example, tend to renovate dining halls in the summer when students are away. That creates peaks in custom work, which makes estimating and production capacity even more important.

speaker: NORA
text: Are there other requirements beyond food safety?

speaker: JAMES
text: Accessibility is one, in general. Serving lines in public settings need to work for people of different heights and for people using wheelchairs, and in the United States there are accessibility rules that apply to public spaces. I won't get into the specifics, because that's a legal question. But it means the height and reach of a counter and shield aren't purely a matter of taste. A supplier that understands those constraints saves the designer work.

speaker: NORA
text: And what does a replacement order look like? Not a big renovation.

speaker: JAMES
text: Let's say a kitchen manager at a corporate cafeteria notices a cracked panel on an existing shield. She doesn't want a new counter. She wants the right replacement part, quickly. The first question is, which model is this, and is the part still available? If the original was bought eight years ago through a dealer who's since changed, that can be surprisingly hard to answer. That's a small, frequent, frustrating problem, and we'll come back to it, because it's one AI can help with.

speaker: NORA
text: How big is the market?

speaker: JAMES
text: We couldn't find a reliable number. There are market research vendors that publish reports on sneeze guards and buffet sneeze guards, but the figures weren't visible to us, and we're not going to quote them. Honestly, in a niche this specialised, top-down market sizes tend to be rough anyway.

speaker: NORA
text: What drives demand, in general?

speaker: JAMES
text: A few things, as inferences rather than sourced figures. Food-safety rules that require shields on displayed food. Renovation and replacement cycles in institutional kitchens. New formats like grab-and-go and food halls. And the general health of foodservice traffic. If more people eat in cafeterias and food bars, more shields are needed.

speaker: NORA
text: And who are the competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a crowded field of well-known foodservice equipment brands. Hatco, which sells the Flav-R-Shield line alongside a broad range of heated food equipment. Advance Tabco, which has its Sleek Shield line and the convertible shield we mentioned, and which a trade headline says added assets from Supreme Metal. Eagle Group, which sells breath shields and countertop shields widely through distributors. Duke Manufacturing, a full-line equipment maker with full-service food shields. Vollrath, with adjustable portable and stationary sneeze guards. And Atlas Metal Industries, with curved tempered-glass food guards.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a lot of big names.

speaker: JAMES
text: And there are more. Bon Chef, APW Wyott, American Metalcraft, Premier Metal and Glass, and English Manufacturing with its VIPER line also show up. We didn't verify who owns each of these companies, so I won't characterise their ownership.

speaker: NORA
text: How does a smaller specialist compete with full-line makers?

speaker: JAMES
text: In my view, with focus and flexibility. A full-line maker can bundle a sneeze guard with a whole serving line, sometimes at an attractive price. A specialist can offer more design options, more customisation, faster turnaround on unusual sizes, and protected features like Brass Smith's adjustable designs. The risk is that if the specialist isn't noticeably better or faster, the bundle wins.

speaker: NORA
text: Any AI-driven competitors?

speaker: JAMES
text: None that we found. We found no AI-specific announcements from any food shield maker. Where AI is changing this category, in our view, is in quoting tools, design and configuration software, and how distributors' websites search and recommend products. Not in the glass itself.

speaker: NORA
text: Is the industry consolidating?

speaker: JAMES
text: There's some evidence, though it's thin. The Advance Tabco asset deal is one example. In general, foodservice equipment has seen plenty of private equity and strategic buyers over the years. For Brass Smith, that's relevant both as a competitive force and as a pool of potential future buyers.

speaker: NORA
text: What about the shape of foodservice itself? Is self-service growing or shrinking?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's mixed, in general. Traditional all-you-can-eat buffets have been under pressure for years. But other self-service and display formats have grown, like food halls, grab-and-go cases, supermarket prepared food bars and corporate micro-markets. And institutional dining, hospitals, universities, workplaces, keeps feeding people at scale. So the question for a shield maker isn't whether display food survives. It's whether it can follow the formats that are growing.

speaker: NORA
text: And corporate cafeterias have had a strange few years.

speaker: JAMES
text: They have, with changes in how often people go into offices. Again, general background. For a supplier, the lesson is to watch which customer segments are renovating and which are holding back, and to point sales effort accordingly. That's actually another use for better data.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make this concrete. Walk me through a project. Invented, not a real customer.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Okay. Imagine a regional hospital, call it Riverside Medical Centre. Its staff cafeteria serves around a thousand meals a day to employees and visitors. The serving line is twenty years old, the shields are scratched, and one section doesn't meet current guidelines. The food services director, let's call her Angela, gets budget approval to renovate over the summer.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And what does she do first?
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: She works with a foodservice consultant, who draws a new layout. A hot food line, a salad bar, a grab-and-go section, and a carving station that's staffed at lunch but self-service at breakfast. The consultant specifies shields and counters, and the hospital's equipment dealer sends the drawings out for quotes from several suppliers, including our hypothetical version of Brass Smith.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What happens inside the supplier?
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Today, in a typical specialist manufacturer, and this is a general picture, an estimator receives a PDF of the layout and some notes. They work out the dimensions of each counter section, the shield type for each position, the materials, the finishes, the hardware. They check whether each shield position meets the certification requirements for the intended service style. They build a bill of materials, estimate labour hours in the shop, add freight and installation, and produce a price and a drawing.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: How long does that take?
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: For a complex project, days, sometimes longer if the estimator has questions and has to wait for answers. And if the consultant changes the layout, which they often do, the estimator starts parts of it again.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Meanwhile, Angela is waiting.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: And the dealer is waiting, and the competitors are quoting too. Now, the carving station is where our hypothetical Brass Smith has an edge. Angela wants one station to switch between self-service and staffed. An adjustable shield with detents solves that neatly. If the estimator spots that and proposes it clearly, it's a differentiator. If the quote just lists a standard shield, the advantage is lost.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: So the quote is also a sales document.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

text: Very much so. A good quote explains why this design solves the customer's problem. And that's hard to do when an estimator is buried in measurements.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

text: Then what?
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

text: If Brass Smith wins, the drawings go to engineering for production detail, the shop builds, and the counters ship in time for the summer install. Any mismatch between quote and reality, a missed hardware item, a wrong dimension, shows up as cost or delay.
chapter: A cafeteria renovation, step by step

text: It's a lot of human translation, from drawing to quote to production.

text: That's the key observation. Every handoff is someone re-reading a drawing and re-entering information. That's exactly where AI and modern configuration tools can help.

text: Publicly, we found nothing. No AI product, no AI partnership, no AI hire and no AI statement. Searches for the company and AI returned no company matches.

text: Not publicly, no. Which is actually the opportunity. In a category where nobody has moved yet, the first supplier to quote custom projects in a day instead of a week, with clean drawings, gets noticed by dealers and consultants. That's a service advantage, not a technology announcement.

text: What about the distributor side?

speaker: JAMES
text: Large online distributors are investing in better search and product recommendations, in general. For suppliers, that means product data matters more. text: Let's talk challenges.

speaker: JAMES
text: First, price pressure on standard products. Standard-size shields are easy to compare online, and big multi-line suppliers can price aggressively or bundle. That's our inference from how the distributor catalogues are structured, but it's a common pattern.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, a manual custom-quote process. We're inferring this, because we didn't see inside the company. But most specialist fabricators quote custom work by hand. That limits how many quotes a team can produce, slows turnaround, and creates errors.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Concentration. Brass Smith appears to rely heavily on one product family, food shields, plus counters. That focus is a strength in a niche, but it limits diversification if demand in that niche softens.

speaker: NORA
text: Fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Visibility. With so little public information, it's hard for anyone outside to judge the business. That includes future buyers. And from what we can see, there's no clear digital or data story yet.

speaker: NORA
text: And people?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a challenge I'd expect, though we can't confirm it. In small manufacturers, estimating and engineering knowledge often sits with a handful of experienced people. They know which configurations meet certification, which hardware works, how long things take in the shop. If one of them leaves, or retires, the business loses capacity and knowledge at the same time. Capturing that knowledge is both an operational and an exit-readiness issue.

speaker: NORA
text: Input costs?

speaker: JAMES
text: In general, glass, acrylic, stainless steel and freight have all seen price swings in recent years. A small manufacturer with long quote-to-delivery times is exposed if it quotes a price today and buys materials months later. That's another argument for faster, data-driven quoting with current costs built in.

speaker: NORA
text: And the owner's clock?

speaker: JAMES
text: Ten and a half years is a long time. In my view, the most important challenge is making the business easy to understand and easy to buy. That means documented intellectual property, clean channel data, and margins by product line.

speaker: NORA
text: Okay, opportunities. You're on the board. Where do you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: The first and biggest is design-to-quote automation for custom counters and shields. A configuration tool that takes dimensions and requirements, generates a design from approved building blocks, produces a bill of materials and a price automatically, and checks the result against certification rules. With AI helping to read customer drawings and draft the configuration.

speaker: NORA
text: Why is that the biggest?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because it hits three things at once. Estimator and engineering hours, which are expensive and scarce. Quote turnaround, which affects how many jobs you win. And accuracy, which affects margins once the job is built. It's also the part of the business that's most differentiated, so improving it compounds the advantage.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Using channel data better. If Brass Smith can see what sells through online distributors, by size, finish and region, it can tune what it stocks and how it prices standard products. Even simple analysis can show which sizes are worth keeping in stock and which should be made to order.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pricing discipline on standard products. Review list price versus what's actually realised in each channel after discounts. In many small manufacturers, discounts creep over time, and nobody has the full picture. AI tools can help analyse quotes and orders to find where margin is leaking.

speaker: NORA
text: Give me an example of margin leaking. Hypothetical, of course.

speaker: JAMES
text: Picture a sales manager, call her Priya, at a small shield maker. Over the years, three dealers have been given special discounts, each for a good reason at the time. One won a big university contract. One promised volume that never quite arrived. One just negotiated hard. Nobody ever reviewed them together. Meanwhile, the cost of glass, metal and freight has gone up.

speaker: NORA
text: So the discounts are still there, but the reason has gone.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Priya asks an AI analysis tool to go through two years of invoices and quotes. It shows her that one dealer gets a deeper discount than the others but orders less, that a popular standard size is now selling below the margin target in one channel, and that custom quotes with rushed timelines tend to come in under the actual cost. None of this needs advanced AI. It needs someone to pull the data together and ask the right questions, and modern tools make that a matter of days rather than months.

speaker: NORA
text: And then she has some awkward conversations.

speaker: JAMES
text: Some, yes. But with evidence. And often the fix is small: retire an old discount, add a rush fee, adjust one price. For a niche manufacturer, a couple of points of margin recovered that way can matter a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: National accounts. You mentioned contract caterers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. In general, large contract foodservice companies run kitchens at hundreds or thousands of client sites, and many have standard design guidelines. Getting specified as a preferred supplier in those guidelines can bring repeat orders across many sites. It's a slow sale with a lot of relationship work, and we don't know whether Brass Smith already has such relationships. But the design-to-quote tool would help here too, because a national account values consistency and speed across many similar projects.

speaker: NORA
text: And growth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cross-selling, for one. If a customer buys shields, can you sell them the counter, the lighting, the accessories, the replacement panels? And geographic expansion through national foodservice dealers and contract caterers, who run kitchens across many sites and could standardise on one supplier.

speaker: NORA
text: Acquisitions?

speaker: JAMES
text: Possibly. The research suggests a bolt-on of a complementary glass or stainless steel fabricator could add capacity and materials capability. That would fit this owner's usual add-on approach, though none has happened so far, as far as we can see. Whether it makes sense this late in a long hold is a judgment for the owner. A buyer might prefer to do that themselves.

speaker: NORA
text: And exit readiness itself as an opportunity?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd frame it that way, yes. Document the patents and what they protect. Build clean data on channels, customers and margins by product line. Show quote turnaround and win rates improving. Each of those makes the business easier to value, and a well-documented business usually sells faster and with fewer surprises.

speaker: NORA
text: Any role for AI in the product itself?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not really, in my view. A food shield doesn't need a chip in it. You could imagine sensors on food bars for temperature or usage, but that's a different product category, and there's no sign Brass Smith wants to go there. The value of AI here is in how the business designs, quotes, sells and plans.

speaker: NORA
text: Remember the cracked panel. What would you do there?

speaker: JAMES
text: A parts and support assistant. The kitchen manager sends a photo of the shield and maybe a label if there is one. The assistant, working from the company's own product history and drawings, identifies the likely model, the right replacement panel and hardware, and drafts a quote or a distributor link. Anything uncertain goes to a person. It's not glamorous, but it turns an annoying hunt into a quick sale, and replacement parts tend to carry good margins.

speaker: NORA
text: And it builds loyalty.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does. The customer remembers who made it easy. And there's a related, simpler win: use AI to improve every product listing on distributor sites. Clear dimensions, materials, certification details, which service styles each shield suits, and good descriptions of why the adjustable designs matter. That's labour that a small team rarely has time for, and AI can draft it quickly for people to check.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's commit. The single best AI bet?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Design-to-quote automation for custom work. Turn a customer's layout and requirements into a draft design, bill of materials and price in hours rather than days, with an estimator reviewing.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: How would you run it?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Days one to thirty: understand the current process. Sit with the estimators, map every step, and collect the last two or three years of quotes, drawings and won or lost outcomes. Measure the baseline: how long a quote takes, how many quotes per estimator per week, the win rate, and how often actual costs differ from the quote.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Data first again.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Always. Days thirty to sixty: build the rule set. Turn the estimators' knowledge into a structured library of approved components, standard sections, hardware and certification rules. Which shield type goes with which service style. Which dimensions are allowed. That library is valuable on its own, because it captures knowledge that otherwise lives in people's heads.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: And then the software?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. Choose a configuration and quoting tool, many exist for manufacturers, and connect it to the library. Use AI to help read incoming drawings and requirements and propose a draft configuration. Days sixty to a hundred: run it in shadow mode on real quotes. The estimator does the quote the usual way, and the tool does it in parallel. Compare time, accuracy and price. Fix the gaps.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: And at day one hundred?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Decide whether to make it the default for certain project types, starting with simpler, repeatable ones, while keeping humans firmly in charge of complex jobs and anything touching certification.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Let's replay Angela's hospital project with that tool in place.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Okay. The dealer sends the consultant's layout to our hypothetical Brass Smith. The estimator, let's call him Tom, uploads the drawing. The AI reads it and proposes a draft: five counter sections, dimensions, a full-service shield on the hot line, a self-service shield on the salad bar, and for the carving station, it flags that the service style changes between breakfast and lunch and suggests the adjustable shield with detents.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: It spots the differentiator.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Because the rule set tells it that a station with two service modes is a fit for that product. Tom checks the dimensions, corrects one section where the drawing was ambiguous, and confirms the finish. The tool builds the bill of materials from the library, prices it using current material costs and shop hours, and produces a clean drawing and a quote that explains the carving station design in plain language.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: How long?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: In our hypothetical, the same day instead of the following week. And because everything was built from the approved library, the shop gets a production-ready list when the job is won, with far less re-entry.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: And if the consultant changes the layout?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Tom updates the draft, the tool recalculates, and a revised quote goes out quickly. That responsiveness is what dealers remember.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: What are the pitfalls?
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: JAMES
text: Three. First, trusting the AI on certification. The rule set must come from people who understand the standards, and anything unusual should be checked by a person. Second, building a beautiful tool nobody uses because it doesn't match how estimators actually work. Involve them from day one. Third, over-scoping. Start with the most common project types and expand.
chapter: The best AI bet and the first 100 days

speaker: NORA
text: Let's widen out. What can other businesses learn here?

speaker: JAMES
text: Four lessons. First, for a custom manufacturer, the quote is the product before the product exists. Speed, clarity and accuracy of quotes often decide who wins. If you want a practical AI starting point, look at your quoting process.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, capture expert knowledge before it walks out of the door. The rule set we described is valuable even without any AI. It makes training easier, reduces errors and protects the business against key-person risk.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, protected design features are worth more when you can explain them. Brass Smith's adjustable shield patents are only valuable if customers understand why adjustability matters. A quoting tool that recognises when the feature fits and explains it turns intellectual property into sales.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, a long hold is an opportunity to get legible. Whatever your ownership, the work of documenting your margins, your channels and your intellectual property pays off when you raise money, bring in a partner or sell. And it makes the business easier to run day to day.

speaker: NORA
text: And for a tiny business, a two-person fabrication shop?

speaker: JAMES
text: Write down your standard designs and your pricing rules. Use a simple quoting template. Try an AI tool to draft quote explanations and customer emails. You don't need custom software to get faster.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a lesson about being quiet for so long?

speaker: JAMES
text: I think there's a fifth lesson in it. A specialist company can rely for years on reputation among a small group of dealers and designers. But the people who specify equipment change, and new ones increasingly research suppliers online and through AI assistants. If almost nothing about you is public, you're relying on memory. A modest investment in clear public information, product specifications and case examples keeps you on the shortlist.

speaker: NORA
text: Even if the customer never reads a press release.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. Nobody buys a sneeze guard because of a press release. But they do buy from the supplier whose specifications show up when they're drawing the plan.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, demand risk. If foodservice moves further away from self-service formats, or if institutional budgets tighten, demand for shields and counters could soften. Two, competitive bundling by large multi-line suppliers, who can sell shields as part of a bigger equipment package. Three, the patents eventually expiring or being designed around.

speaker: NORA
text: And an AI-specific risk?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, an interesting one. AI-driven configurators and general design tools could lower the barrier for smaller local fabricators. If anyone with a good tool can produce a professional custom quote quickly, the speed advantage we've been describing narrows. That's an argument for moving early, and for leaning on certification and protected designs, which tools alone can't copy.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owner?

speaker: JAMES
text: Timing. After a decade, the window to show improvements before a sale is limited. If the operating story isn't ready, a buyer prices in the uncertainty.

speaker: NORA
text: Are there risks in the AI tools themselves?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. A quoting tool that produces a wrong dimension or the wrong shield type for a service style creates real cost, because custom work is hard to rework once it's built. Worse, a configuration that doesn't meet certification could cause problems at inspection for the customer. So the tool has to be constrained to approved components and rules, and every quote that goes out should be reviewed by someone accountable for it.

speaker: NORA
text: And the data the tool learns from?

speaker: JAMES
text: Old quotes include mistakes and one-off deals. If you train on them blindly, you copy the mistakes. That's why the first phase is about building a clean rule set with the estimators, rather than just pointing a model at the archive. There's also a basic security point. Customer drawings for hospitals and other institutions can be sensitive, so any tool should be chosen with care about where that data goes.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three things. First, any ownership change or sale process, which after ten and a half years wouldn't be surprising. Second, any new product announcements, especially around adjustable or convertible shields, where competition is active. Third, any sign of investment in quoting, configuration or digital tools, or a leadership hire in operations or technology.

speaker: NORA
text: And something that would worry you?

speaker: JAMES
text: Continued silence right up to a sale. Not because silence is bad in itself, but because it would suggest the work of making the business legible hasn't been done.

speaker: NORA
text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: NORA
text: What does Brass Smith sell, in five words?

speaker: JAMES
text: Glass that keeps food safe.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Patented adjustable food shield designs, plus custom counter know-how.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: Probably a manual, slow custom-quoting process, though that's our inference.

speaker: NORA
text: Best AI bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Design-to-quote automation for custom projects.

speaker: NORA
text: Second best?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pricing and stocking analytics on standard products sold through distributors.

speaker: NORA
text: Does a sneeze guard need AI in it?

speaker: JAMES
text: No. The AI belongs in the quote, not the glass.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a custom manufacturer should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Time how long your last ten quotes took, and how many you won.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Cautiously optimistic about the niche. Uncertain about the company, simply because we know so little.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me sum up. Brass Smith Innovations is a Denver company that designs and builds food shields and custom counters for institutional foodservice, selling through distributors like WebstaurantStore and directly. Levine Leichtman bought it in March 2016, with senior debt from Madison Capital Funding, and has held it for about ten and a half years, with no add-ons or news that we could find in the last two years. Its distinctive asset is a family of patents on adjustable food shields. It competes with big names like Hatco, Advance Tabco, Eagle, Duke and Vollrath. We found no AI activity. Our view is that the best opportunity is design-to-quote automation for custom work, built on a captured rule set of the company's own expertise, with better pricing and channel data close behind. All of that also makes the business easier to understand and to sell.

speaker: JAMES
text: Well put. And my closing thought is that AI isn't only for companies with software products or huge data sets. A small manufacturer that turns a week-long quote into a same-day quote has used AI exactly where it counts, in front of the customer, at the moment they decide.
